author: Cicero
rationale: Cicero's most famous speech. Periodic prose at its highest pitch. The speech that defined Roman oratory.
description: You will read the entire first Catilinarian oration: Cicero's denunciation of the conspirator Catiline, delivered in the Senate in 63 BCE. This is the speech that begins 'Quousque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?' — How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience? It is the model of Latin periodic structure, rhetorical force, and invective.
learning_outcomes: Read and translate the entire In Catilinam I (c. 6,500 words) with notes.
Recognize and analyze Ciceronian periodic structure.
Identify rhetorical devices: anaphora, tricolon, chiasmus, apostrophe.
Translate any fifty-word passage from the speech at sight without notes.
Discuss Cicero's argumentative strategy and political context in writing.

weekly_plan.focus: The opening: Quousque tandem. Cicero establishes the enormity of Catiline's crime.
Cicero recounts the conspiracy and the Senate's prior inaction.
The historical precedents: how past consuls dealt with traitors.
Cicero's defense of his own hesitation and clemency.
The call to leave: Cicero urges Catiline to depart from Rome.
The personification of Rome: the city itself speaks to Catiline.
The conspiracy unmasked: names and plans revealed.
Final appeal to the Senate and the people.
Read the first half again at speed.
Read the second half again at speed.
Read the entire speech aloud in one sitting.

recommended_resources: Shackleton Bailey, D.R. (ed.), Cicero: Catilinarians (Loeb Classical Library)
Dyck, Andrew R., Cicero: Catilinarians (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics)
Gotoff, H.C., Cicero's Elegant Style: An Analysis of the Pro Archia
capstone_prep: In the final two weeks, focus on sight translation. Take random fifty-word passages from the speech and translate them without notes. Aim for fluency, not word-for-word accuracy. On the capstone exam you will see one passage from In Catilinam I that you have not prepared.
